passages.title: Two paths
passages.summary: The poem compares a person who follows God’s teaching with windblown chaff.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does the tree help explain a life shaped by daily learning?

contextNote.title: Two images frame the collection
contextNote.text: A rooted tree and scattered chaff give two ways of life different futures. The poem describes habits before their outcomes. This opening asks readers to consider how repeated attention shapes a life.

passages.title: Kings oppose the Lord’s chosen king
passages.summary: Rulers resist the Lord and his anointed king. The poem calls them to serve with care.
passages.uncertainty: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the anointed king with Jesus Christ. Anointing uses oil to mark a chosen role. What warning does the poem give rulers?

contextNote.title: Royal language ends with a warning
contextNote.text: The rebellious rulers hear a claim of divine authority over kingship. Their final instruction calls for wisdom rather than continued resistance. Power in this poem requires an answer to a higher claim.

passages.title: Rest while enemies surround the speaker
passages.summary: The speaker faces many enemies but sleeps with trust in God’s protection.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: What makes the speaker able to rest while danger remains?

contextNote.title: Sleep becomes evidence of endurance
contextNote.text: The speaker faces many opponents but still lies down and wakes. This ordinary action gives trust a bodily form. The final blessing extends the personal appeal to the whole people.

passages.title: An evening prayer for peace
passages.summary: The speaker asks for an answer, challenges falsehood, and lies down in peace.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: Which sources of security does the speaker compare?

contextNote.title: Joy uses a different measure
contextNote.text: The speaker compares inward gladness with successful harvests. Material abundance no longer supplies the only measure of security. The closing sleep gives that difference an ordinary setting.

passages.title: A morning prayer for guidance
passages.summary: The speaker asks God to hear and lead. Deceitful enemies threaten the path ahead.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: How can truthful speech help someone choose a safe path?

contextNote.title: Morning organizes a waiting prayer
contextNote.text: The speaker directs words toward God at the start of the day. Requests for guidance follow descriptions of harmful speech. The poem makes waiting and careful direction part of facing a dangerous public world.

passages.title: A prayer through tears
passages.summary: The speaker asks for mercy during weakness, fear, and sleepless grief.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: What help does the speaker seek during sleepless grief?

contextNote.title: Tears give the complaint a place
contextNote.text: The bed becomes soaked through repeated weeping. This image places the prayer inside an exhausting night. The closing confidence changes its direction without making that earlier suffering imaginary.

passages.title: A plea for a fair judgment
passages.summary: The speaker offers to accept judgment if guilty. The prayer asks God to stop violence.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the speaker invite examination of his own conduct?

contextNote.title: The appeal includes a test of innocence
contextNote.text: The speaker names possible wrongdoing before asking for rescue. This condition makes judgment apply to him as well as enemies. The requested judgment could therefore examine the speaker’s own actions.

passages.title: Human life beneath the stars
passages.summary: The speaker marvels at the heavens and humanity’s place among God’s works.
passages.uncertainty: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects creation with human worth. What care for other creatures does the poem describe?

contextNote.title: Smallness and dignity belong together
contextNote.text: The heavens make human beings seem small. Yet the poem describes people receiving honor and responsibility. The repeated opening and ending surround this tension with praise.

passages.title: Praise for justice against oppression
passages.summary: The speaker praises God’s judgment and asks for help against enemies.
passages.uncertainty: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

lds.text: How does the prayer protect the hope of poor people?

contextNote.title: Public praise includes forgotten people
contextNote.text: Thanksgiving for judgment turns toward the needs of poor people. Their apparent disappearance must not become permanent neglect. The closing request asks nations to remember the limits of human power.

passages.title: Why does the oppressor seem safe?
passages.summary: The speaker describes hidden attacks on the poor and asks God to intervene.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: What harm does the oppressor try to keep hidden?

contextNote.title: The enemy’s claim drives the prayer
contextNote.text: The violent person acts as though God does not notice. The speaker answers by asking God to see and act. Repeated attention to vulnerable people gives that disagreement concrete stakes.

passages.title: Trust when the foundations fail
passages.summary: Others urge flight. The speaker looks to the Lord, who sees human conduct.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: What remains dependable when familiar supports fail?

contextNote.title: An offered escape is challenged
contextNote.text: The speaker receives advice to flee when public order fails. He answers by locating judgment beyond the ruined foundations. The poem presents competing responses to danger rather than a report of safe conditions.

passages.title: Help when honest speech disappears
passages.summary: The speaker contrasts flattery and boastful words with God’s promise to protect the poor.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does the promise to the poor differ from flattery?

contextNote.title: Words can either exploit or protect
contextNote.text: Flattering mouths promise power over other people. Divine speech answers the cries of those being harmed. The contrast asks whose words deserve trust when public language becomes a means of control.

passages.title: How long must the speaker wait?
passages.summary: The speaker asks how long God will remain distant, then recalls his kindness.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: What changes between the opening question and the closing song?

contextNote.title: Repeated questions stretch the wait
contextNote.text: The opening returns several times to the length of abandonment. A request then leads to trust and song. The change concerns the speaker’s address, without naming an event that solved the danger.

passages.title: Corruption and the hope of rescue
passages.summary: The poem describes widespread wrongdoing and people who consume others without concern.
passages.uncertainty: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

lds.text: Whose rescue does the closing prayer seek?

contextNote.title: A judgment about humanity becomes social
contextNote.text: The poem connects corruption with consuming the people as food. Its diagnosis therefore reaches treatment of neighbors, not only stated belief. The ending seeks a shared restoration beyond an individual escape.

passages.title: Who may stay in God’s presence?
passages.summary: The poem names honesty, fair dealings, and refusal to exploit others.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: Which daily choices does the poem connect with worship?

contextNote.title: Entry depends on ordinary conduct
contextNote.text: A question about dwelling in God’s presence receives answers about speech and transactions. The list carries worship into relationships outside the sanctuary. Access is measured through conduct rather than a description of ceremonial clothing.

passages.title: A secure portion
passages.summary: The speaker rejects other gods and finds security in the Lord’s counsel and presence.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: What gives the speaker a sense of belonging?

contextNote.title: Inheritance gives security a shape
contextNote.text: Boundary lines and a portion describe what the speaker has received. These images make dependence on God resemble a secure place. The final path of life extends that relation beyond present possessions.

passages.title: A plea for protection from violent people
passages.summary: The speaker asks God to examine the heart and shelter it from enemies.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does the speaker connect protection with an examined heart?

contextNote.title: Protection becomes intimate
contextNote.text: The speaker asks for care through images of an eye and sheltering wings. Those images answer violent people who surround him. The closing desire for God’s presence contrasts with enemies satisfied by present abundance.

passages.title: Rescue pictured through storm and battle
passages.summary: The speaker recalls God’s rescue through earthquake, storm, and strength against enemies.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: How do the storm images describe the force of rescue?

contextNote.title: Rescue is described through an overwhelming landscape
contextNote.text: Storm, shaking earth, and deep waters enlarge the speaker’s danger. Deliverance then becomes training, strength, and victory. The poem moves between weakness and royal power rather than keeping one unchanging speaker’s position.

passages.title: The heavens and God’s teaching
passages.summary: The skies declare God’s glory. His teaching guides the speaker toward honest words and thoughts.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does attention to creation lead toward examining words and thoughts?

contextNote.title: The poem narrows from skies to speech
contextNote.text: The heavens declare glory before the poem praises divine instruction. It ends with the speaker’s own words and inward thought. This movement brings the vast world into a personal request for acceptable conduct.

passages.title: A prayer for the king before danger
passages.summary: The people ask God to accept the king’s offerings and answer his plans.
passages.uncertainty: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

lds.text: Why do the people trust God more than horses and chariots?

contextNote.title: A community speaks before a battle
contextNote.text: The repeated wishes address another person’s need and hoped-for victory. Chariots and horses then become a contrast with reliance on God. The final shared call reveals that the prayer is wider than one voice.

passages.title: Thanks for the king’s deliverance
passages.summary: The poem celebrates the king’s joy, life, honor, and rescue from enemies.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does the king respond to the help he receives?

contextNote.title: Royal praise locates strength elsewhere
contextNote.text: The king’s joy begins with strength received from God. Descriptions of victory follow that dependence. The poem’s royal confidence therefore rests on a gift rather than the king’s independent power.

passages.title: Abandonment, suffering, and praise
passages.summary: The speaker cries about distance, mockery, and physical danger. The ending calls others to praise.
passages.uncertainty: The named areas give context to the song. They do not form a reconstructed travel route.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects this suffering with Jesus Christ’s crucifixion. Crucifixion means death on a cross. How does the prayer change toward its end?

contextNote.title: A song can move without erasing its beginning
contextNote.text: The opening gives abandonment a direct address to God. Later verses turn toward praise and a wider gathered people. Read the movement across the whole song. The ending does not mean the first cry was false. Prayer can hold distress and renewed hope within one work.

passages.title: The Lord as shepherd and host
passages.summary: The speaker describes guidance, danger, welcome, and a place in the Lord’s house.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses the shepherd image to study Christ’s care.

contextNote.title: The shelter changes from field to table
contextNote.text: The shepherd image gives movement and protection a pastoral setting. A prepared meal then presents welcome despite surrounding enemies. These connected images describe provision without claiming that danger has vanished.

passages.title: Who may enter before the King of glory?
passages.summary: The poem asks who may approach God. Its final call welcomes the King of glory.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects clean hands and hearts with temple worship. Which actions does the poem require?

contextNote.title: Ownership leads to a question about access
contextNote.text: The opening places the whole earth under God’s rule. The next question asks who can approach the holy place. Its answer joins clean conduct with the later welcome of the King of glory.

passages.title: Guidance, forgiveness, and loneliness
passages.summary: The speaker asks God to teach, forgive earlier sins, and relieve distress.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does admitting failure make room for learning?

contextNote.title: Memory can wound or restore
contextNote.text: The speaker asks God to remember mercy rather than youthful sins. Requests for instruction then join confession with a desired future. The ending moves the individual need into Israel’s wider troubles.

passages.title: Integrity and love for worship
passages.summary: The speaker asks God to examine the heart and refuses fellowship with harmful people.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies preparation for temple worship. Which harmful actions does the speaker refuse to join?

contextNote.title: A claim of integrity leads toward worship
contextNote.text: The speaker asks for examination before describing movement around the altar. Refusal of harmful company belongs within that approach. The poem combines a personal defense with the desire to praise among others.

passages.title: Seeking God’s face amid fear
passages.summary: The speaker wants to dwell near God and asks for help against enemies.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: What kind of courage does waiting require?

contextNote.title: Confidence turns into a request
contextNote.text: The opening declares safety and the desire for God’s house. Later lines plead against abandonment and ask for guidance. Reading both movements prevents confidence from being mistaken for the absence of fear.

passages.title: Do not remain silent
passages.summary: The speaker asks God to hear and avoid judging him with deceitful people.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the prayer widen from one speaker to all the people?

contextNote.title: Silence feels like descent
contextNote.text: The speaker links an unanswered prayer with joining the dead. The later blessing answers that fear through heard petition. The ending asks for shared care using the new image of a shepherd.

passages.title: The Lord’s voice over the storm
passages.summary: The poem describes the Lord’s voice shaking waters, trees, mountains, and wilderness.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does the ending change the mood of the storm?

contextNote.title: A storm supplies the poem’s repeated voice
contextNote.text: The voice of God moves across waters, trees, and wilderness. The repetition makes power audible through the imagined storm. Its final gift of peace answers the force displayed throughout the poem.

passages.title: Mourning becomes dancing
passages.summary: The speaker recalls rescue from death, a time of confidence, and renewed praise.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: What did the speaker learn when earlier confidence failed?

contextNote.title: Past security receives a correction
contextNote.text: The speaker remembers believing prosperity could never fail. God’s hidden face changes that confidence into fear and petition. Restored joy therefore follows an account of mistaken self-assurance.

passages.title: Entrusting life to God
passages.summary: The speaker describes traps, shame, and rejection while asking for refuge.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects this prayer with Jesus Christ’s words. What help does the speaker still request?

contextNote.title: Trust remains inside a threatened life
contextNote.text: The speaker describes public suspicion and fear on every side. His surrender of spirit and time answers that setting. The closing address invites others into trust without removing the poem’s particular danger.

passages.title: Confession after the weight of silence
passages.summary: The speaker describes the strain of hiding sin and the relief of confession.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does confession change the burden of silence?

contextNote.title: Silence and confession have different bodily effects
contextNote.text: Unspoken wrongdoing becomes exhaustion and dryness. Acknowledgment then makes room for forgiveness and instruction. The poem presents confession as a change in relation rather than only naming an offense.

passages.title: Praise for the maker who sees all people
passages.summary: The poem celebrates creation and God’s knowledge of human hearts.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: What can an army fail to provide?

contextNote.title: A hymn tests familiar signs of strength
contextNote.text: The opening calls for a harp and a new song. Its praise of creation then turns toward armies, warriors, and horses. These visible powers cannot guarantee rescue. The closing hope brings musical praise into the community's present need.

passages.title: Learning to seek peace
passages.summary: The speaker praises rescue and calls others to truthful speech, goodness, and peace.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects the unbroken bones with Jesus Christ. What does the poem teach about seeking peace?

contextNote.title: Personal testimony becomes instruction
contextNote.text: The speaker’s rescued life begins the praise. Invitations to taste, seek, and learn then address other people. The poem turns remembered help into teaching about speech, peace, and vulnerability.

passages.title: A plea against false accusations
passages.summary: The speaker asks for defense against enemies who repay care with hostility.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does earlier kindness make the enemies’ conduct especially painful?

contextNote.title: Friendship intensifies the injury
contextNote.text: The speaker recalls mourning for people who now rejoice over his trouble. Their behavior makes the conflict a betrayal of prior care. Repeated promises of public praise keep that personal wound connected with an audience.

passages.title: Wickedness and the reach of kindness
passages.summary: The poem contrasts inward wrongdoing with God’s kindness, faithfulness, and care for living creatures.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does the poem contrast deceit with the reach of kindness?

contextNote.title: Two landscapes describe opposing lives
contextNote.text: The opening describes wrongdoing through a person’s thoughts and actions. Divine mercy then expands through skies, mountains, shelter, and water. The change in scale gives the speaker’s requested refuge a rich setting.

passages.title: Do not envy the success of wrongdoing
passages.summary: The poem urges patience, generosity, and trust when harmful people seem to prosper.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: What might envy of harmful people make someone overlook?

contextNote.title: Waiting interrupts envy
contextNote.text: The poem repeatedly warns against anger at prosperous wrongdoers. Its instruction stretches attention toward consequences beyond present success. That form matters because the temptation begins with what the reader can currently see.

passages.title: Pain, guilt, and distant friends
passages.summary: The speaker describes illness, wrongdoing, and companions standing far away.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: What help is missing when companions stand far away?

contextNote.title: Bodily pain and isolation reinforce each other
contextNote.text: The speaker describes injured flesh before naming distant friends and active enemies. Confession does not remove his need for company and rescue. The ending remains an urgent appeal rather than reporting recovery.

passages.title: The brevity of life
passages.summary: The speaker struggles to remain silent and reflects on how quickly human life passes.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does a short life change the value of stored wealth?

contextNote.title: Guarded speech turns into a question about life
contextNote.text: The speaker’s effort to remain silent increases inward distress. He then asks to understand how brief life is. The complaint joins restraint, mortality, and a desire for relief before death.

passages.title: Rescue followed by a new appeal
passages.summary: The speaker recalls rescue and public praise, then asks for help in fresh distress.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does earlier rescue lead to another request for help?

contextNote.title: A rescued voice still needs help
contextNote.text: The opening remembers being lifted from a pit and given a song. Later lines describe fresh trouble and ask God not to delay. Remembered deliverance therefore supplies grounds for petition rather than an ending to all need.

passages.title: Care for the weak and betrayal
passages.summary: The speaker praises care for the poor and asks for help amid illness and betrayal.
passages.uncertainty: The prayer supplies no secure place for a map marker.

steps.title: A song can move without erasing its beginning
steps.text: The opening gives abandonment a direct address to God. Later verses turn toward praise and a wider gathered people. Read the movement across the whole song. The ending does not mean the first cry was false. Prayer can hold distress and renewed hope within one work.

steps.title: Some prayers end without visible relief
steps.text: This song closes with isolation rather than a clear recovery. Its presence beside praise songs gives unresolved grief a place in worship. The speaker still addresses God throughout the complaint. Read that continued address as part of the poem’s action. The collection does not require every prayer to end in comfort.

steps.title: Exile changes what a song can do
steps.text: The captors request music from people who have lost their home. The question about singing links worship with place and forced performance. The final anger must be read beside that loss. A Babylonian hymn tablet provides a comparison with another tradition of sacred songs. It does not prove that this psalm borrowed from that hymn.
